title: Yahrzeit
hookLine: on the anniversary of a death, a candle burns through the day

lines: A WHITE CANDLE IN A PLAIN GLASS.
EVERY TIME THEY PASS, A FACE.
cards: On a kitchen counter, away from the curtains, sits a short white candle in a plain glass. It was lit at sundown. Nobody is eating by its light, and nobody will blow it out.
It will burn through the night and the whole next day, until it goes out on its own. The person who lit it walks past it making coffee, answering the phone, while the kids argue about homework.
Every time they pass, they remember a face. A parent, maybe.

teach.h: A YIDDISH WORD FOR A YEARLY DAY.
teach.b: Yahrzeit is a Yiddish word, the word Ashkenazi Jews use for the anniversary of a death. Sephardi families have their own names for the same day. It's kept for parents above all, and for others a person mourns.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE LAMP.
teach.b: The tradition points to a verse in Proverbs: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A small flame, steady and quiet, stands in for a life.

teach.h: THE HEBREW DATE, NOT THE WALL CALENDAR.
teach.b: The yahrzeit is traditionally kept on the date of death in the Hebrew calendar, not the everyday one. The Hebrew calendar's months follow the moon, so the day slides around on the wall calendar from year to year.
Families keep a note of it, or a synagogue sends a reminder; remembering takes a little planning.

On the day, mourners often go to synagogue to say the mourner's Kaddish with a minyan, the ten from yesterday. The Kaddish is a prayer in Aramaic, and it doesn't mention death at all. It praises God's name.
Mourners stand in front of the community and say, in effect, we are still here, and we still praise. Some people visit the grave. Some give to charity in the person's name.
Some study a passage of the Mishnah; tradition notes that the Hebrew letters of Mishnah can be rearranged to spell neshamah, soul.
And some just sit with the candle, and tell a story about the person to anyone who'll listen.
One thing is shared: the date comes back each year, and someone keeps it.

how: On the yahrzeit, kept on the Hebrew date of death, Jews light a memorial candle at sundown that burns through the next day, and mourners often say the Kaddish in synagogue with a minyan, visit the grave, give charity or study in the person's memory.

games.q: your mother's yahrzeit is coming. this year, the Hebrew date of her death falls weeks away from the date on your wall calendar. when do you light the candle?
o: on the date on the wall calendar.
on the Hebrew date, starting at sundown the evening before.
whenever the week is quiet enough.
games.why: traditionally, the yahrzeit follows the Hebrew calendar. the candle is lit at sundown, when the Hebrew day begins, and it burns through the next day.

practice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it now; if not, picture the flame.
Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you loved or whose life mattered to you from afar, and let the small, steady flame stand for them.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words, or say the Kaddish later with a congregation; if not, simply say their name once, out loud.

wordCard.voice: Yahrzeit. The yearly anniversary of a death, kept on the Hebrew date with a candle that burns through the day, and often with the Kaddish. Today's word.

orig.note: Yiddish: the yearly anniversary of a death.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the date. The candle goes out on its own; the remembering doesn't. Be gentle with yourself today.
